title: Soil Properties as Key Drivers of Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Climate Change
source: International Journal of experimental research and review
summary: Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from the agricultural sector play a significant role in global warming and climate change. Soils act as both sources and sinks of greenhouse gases (GHGs), including nitrous oxide (N2O), carbon dioxide (CO2) an
content: Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from the agricultural sector play a significant role in global warming and climate change. Soils act as both sources and sinks of greenhouse gases (GHGs), including nitrous oxide (N2O), carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4). While previous studies have largely examined the contribution of agriculture and land-use change to anthropogenic GHG emissions, the contribution of specific soil properties to GHG emissions remains less clear. Therefore, this review synthesizes previous studies not only on broader soil properties but also highlights specific soil variables and their interactions within these broader categories that contribute to individual GHGs and regulate their production and emissions. We conclude that soil physical, biological, and chemical properties are important drivers of GHG emissions. Physical properties include soil temperature, bulk density, water content, soil structure, texture and porosity. Biological properties, particularly biological processes and chemical properties, including soil pH, organic matter, soil carbon, cation exchange capacity (CEC) and micronutrient availability, interact to regulate GHG production, consumption and emissions. Understanding these soil-specific controls is therefore essential for developing effective and context-specific strategies for reducing GHG emissions and enhancing the mitigation potential of agricultural soils.

title: YASHIL IQTISODIYOTGA O‘TISHNING GERMANIYA MODELI VA UNDAN O‘ZBEKISTONDA FOYDALANISH IMKONIYATLARI
summary: This article analyzes the German model of transition to a green economy and the possibilities of its application in Uzbekistan. The study examines the main directions determining Germany’s green transformation, particularly the development
content: This article analyzes the German model of transition to a green economy and the possibilities of its application in Uzbekistan. The study examines the main directions determining Germany’s green transformation, particularly the development of renewable energy, the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions, the development of the GreenTech sector, green financing, and green hydrogen technologies. Based on Germany’s statistical indicators in these areas, the energy, environmental, economic, and financial outcomes of the green transformation are assessed. The study concludes by identifying the aspects of Germany’s experience that can be applied under the conditions of Uzbekistan and presents relevant conclusions and recommendations.

title: Window dressing green: how performance aspiration gaps drive symbolic environmental management in the textile value chain
summary: Addressing the recurring phenomenon of symbolic environmental management in which firms decouple environmental commitments from actual practice, this study analyses the impact of performance aspiration gaps on such strategic behaviours with
content: Addressing the recurring phenomenon of symbolic environmental management in which firms decouple environmental commitments from actual practice, this study analyses the impact of performance aspiration gaps on such strategic behaviours within the textile industry value chain. Based on a sample of listed companies in China’s textile industry value chain from 2015 to 2023, we empirically test these relationships and find that performance aspiration gaps significantly induce symbolic environmental management in firms within the textile industry value chain. Specifically, firms are more likely to engage in high-profile disclosure without substantive implementation when facing performance shortfalls. Furthermore, this effect is time-dependent; the longer the performance aspiration gap, the more significant its impact on symbolic environmental management. Mechanism tests indicate that performance aspiration gaps drive this behaviour by exacerbating financing constraints and intensifying managerial myopia. Heterogeneity analysis further reveals that the inducement effect of performance aspiration gaps on symbolic environmental management is more pronounced in firms located in regions with lower marketisation levels and weaker environmental regulations, as well as in firms with poorer actual ESG performance. This study contributes to the literature by uncovering the internal micro-mechanisms of environmental decoupling under performance pressure.

title: Technological evolution of proton exchange membrane fuel cell systems: a main path analysis
summary: Hydrogen fuel cells are a key technology for achieving carbon neutrality and supporting the global energy transition. As research has evolved from electrochemical materials to intelligent energy systems, understanding the long-term technolo
content: Hydrogen fuel cells are a key technology for achieving carbon neutrality and supporting the global energy transition. As research has evolved from electrochemical materials to intelligent energy systems, understanding the long-term technological evolution of hydrogen fuel cell technologies has become increasingly important. However, existing review studies primarily summarize research themes or publication trends and provide limited insight into knowledge evolution. This study reconstructs the technological evolution of hydrogen fuel cell research using 1,209 journal articles retrieved from the Science Citation Index Expanded (SCI-EXPANDED) of the Web of Science Core Collection (1995–2025). A citation network was established, and Search Path Link Count (SPLC)-based Main Path Analysis together with Key-route Analysis was employed to identify dominant knowledge diffusion trajectories and major technological transitions. The results reveal four major stages of technological evolution: (1) PEMFC design and manufacturing, (2) durability enhancement and high-temperature operation, (3) hybrid fuel cell system integration for fuel cell hybrid electric vehicles (FCHEVs), and (4) AI-enabled energy management and intelligent operational control. These citation-based trajectories suggest a progressive transition from component-level electrochemical engineering toward integrated and intelligent hydrogen energy systems. The findings provide an evidence-based understanding of historical knowledge evolution and offer valuable guidance for future research and technology planning. Nevertheless, the results should be interpreted in light of the study’s reliance on the Web of Science Core Collection and the inherent citation lag, which may underrepresent recently published research.

title: A study on the solidification behaviour of Al–Cr–La alloys in the aluminium-rich region
source: Journal of Thermal Analysis and Calorimetry
summary: Abstract This study examines the solidification behaviour of Al–Cr–La alloys, reflecting the increasing use of rare-earth elements to enhance the properties of aluminium alloys. The research aims to determine how the new ternary phase Al 20
content: Abstract This study examines the solidification behaviour of Al–Cr–La alloys, reflecting the increasing use of rare-earth elements to enhance the properties of aluminium alloys. The research aims to determine how the new ternary phase Al 20 Cr 2 La, formed by the addition of La, influences the solidification process. This fundamental understanding is essential before these alloys can be developed for high-performance applications. Ten alloys with varying Cr (0.03–2.0 at%) and La (0.03–1.0 at%) contents were produced using an arc melter. After annealing at 600 °C for 600 h, their solidification and microstructure were analysed using DSC and SEM. In alloys with higher Cr content, solidification begins with the Al 45 Cr 7 phase, followed by the ternary Al 20 Cr 2 La phase, then (Al), and finally a mixture of (Al) + Al 11 La 3 . Thus, the first series of alloys (samples A–E with varying Cr contents) exhibit four phases: Al 45 Cr 7 , Al 20 Cr 2 La, (Al), and Al 11 La 3 . (Al) is present in the matrix and mixed with Al 11 La 3 , while the ternary Al 20 Cr 2 La phase is observed around the binary Al 45 Cr 7 phase. Second series (samples F–J with varying La contents), solidification also begins with the binary Al 45 Cr 7 phase, followed by the ternary Al 20 Cr 2 La phase and (Al), and finally the (Al) + Al 11 La 3 mixture. In this case, the microstructure of samples with increased La content (F–J) consists of the ternary Al 20 Cr 2 La phase, the (Al) + Al 11 La 3 mixture, and an (Al) matrix.

title: Phytic acid-cerium composite coatings modified with silver nanoparticles for corrosion protection and antibacterial activity on AZ91D Mg alloy
summary: This work presents the synthesis and evaluation of phytic acid–cerium composite coatings with anticorrosive properties on AZ91D magnesium alloy. The coatings were formed by a simple one-step electrochemical process from a single solution co
content: This work presents the synthesis and evaluation of phytic acid–cerium composite coatings with anticorrosive properties on AZ91D magnesium alloy. The coatings were formed by a simple one-step electrochemical process from a single solution combining phytic acid and cerium ions, aiming to enhance corrosion resistance in a simulated physiological environment. The influence of two different cerium salt concentrations in the phytic acid coating bath on the corrosion behavior was investigated. The results demonstrate that the incorporation of 10 mM Ce(NO₃)₃ into the phytic acid bath reduces the corrosion current density by approximately five orders of magnitude compared to the uncoated alloy. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy revealed the development of a self-healing behavior, attributed to the deposition of corrosion products and cerium-based compounds on the substrate surface. Furthermore, the modification of the phytic acid-cerium coating with silver nanoparticles imparted notable antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus . Overall, this study reports the formation of a phytic acid–cerium composite coating obtained in a single step from a combined solution and applied to a magnesium-based alloy, offering a simple strategy for corrosion protection and functional surface modification of Mg alloys.

title: Hydromechanical Behaviour of Intact and Recompacted Crushed Caprock for Underground CO2 Storage
summary: Abstract This work investigates the hydromechanical behaviour of Opalinus Clay (OPA) shale as a caprock material for geological storage of CO $$_2$$ 2 . In addition to intact OPA, the hydromechanical response of crushed material is evaluate
content: Abstract This work investigates the hydromechanical behaviour of Opalinus Clay (OPA) shale as a caprock material for geological storage of CO $$_2$$ 2 . In addition to intact OPA, the hydromechanical response of crushed material is evaluated to simulate damaged zones around injection wells or faults. An initial experimental campaign was conducted to establish a recompaction protocol and to determine the main hydromechanical properties of crushed OPA, from both sandy and shaly-rich facies. The acquired hydromechanical and sealing properties of recompacted OPA were then compared to intact sandy-rich OPA under the same effective stress conditions. Although comparable bulk density and porosity were achieved, the recompacted material remained significantly weaker, exhibiting an elastic modulus approximately one order of magnitude lower than that of the intact material. The water permeability of the recompacted samples approximately one order of magnitude higher, with an average value of $$4 \times 10^{-19}$$ 4 × 10 - 19 m $$^2$$ 2 , compared with $$2 \times 10^{-19}$$ 2 × 10 - 19 m $$^2$$ 2 for intact sandy-rich OPA. Constant rate gaseous CO $$_2$$ 2 injection tests resulted in comparable levels of breakthrough pressure, with average pressure equal to 1.60 MPa for the recompacted and 2.17 MPa for the intact OPA material. To further analyse and interpret the hydromechanical and sealing response of the caprock material, X-ray tomographies of intact, pre-fissured and crushed OPA samples were acquired at different levels of confining and pore water pressure. The observed microstructural evolution of crushed OPA during mechanical compaction and water resaturation, highlighted the role of mineralogical and structural heterogeneity in the material’s self-sealing response.

title: Ultrafast laser–material interactions in commercial aluminium alloys: Ablation threshold, material removal mechanisms, and surface chemistry under femtosecond laser irradiation
summary: As industries such as aerospace, automotive, and marine adopt new materials and designs, the need arises for advanced processing techniques which can shape this material while achieving required part properties. Aluminum alloys, widely used
content: As industries such as aerospace, automotive, and marine adopt new materials and designs, the need arises for advanced processing techniques which can shape this material while achieving required part properties. Aluminum alloys, widely used for their low weight, high strength, and corrosion resistance, still face limitations in hardness, wear resistance, and surface fouling. Surface laser processing offers a method to overcome these limitations. Specifically, femtosecond laser ablation offers a high-precision, low-defect method for surface texturing, capable of producing nano- and microscale features. This study investigates the femtosecond laser ablation threshold and material removal behavior of four aluminum alloys—99% pure Al, AA6061, AA7075, and Scalmalloy®—using a 4 W, 400 fs pulse laser at repetition rates up to 1 MHz. The results show significant variability in feature sizes, with AA6061 exhibiting the largest crater diameters depth for and pure Al displaying the greatest ablation depth (up to 4.1 μm) for the same process parameters. Increasing laser power resulted in a linear increase in ablation depth, while pulse repetition rate exhibited an inverse linear trend with depth, contrary to what would be expected from conventional laser processing. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) revealed that laser processing had minimal impact on surface chemistry, with aluminum oxide remaining the dominant component. Differences in physical properties, such as conductivity, reflectivity, and melting point, were identified as the key factors influencing ablation behaviour. These findings underscore the need for material-specific optimization when developing femtosecond laser-based processing techniques for aluminum alloys.

title: Optimizing decentralized wastewater allocation to urban green spaces in the water scarce megacity of Tehran
summary: Abstract Water scarcity is among the most pressing global challenges, and conventional systems increasingly fail to secure reliable urban water supplies. Reusing municipal wastewater for irrigation offers a sustainable, low-cost option for
content: Abstract Water scarcity is among the most pressing global challenges, and conventional systems increasingly fail to secure reliable urban water supplies. Reusing municipal wastewater for irrigation offers a sustainable, low-cost option for sustaining urban green spaces, the largest non-potable water users in arid cities. This study develops a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model to evaluate a decentralized wastewater-reuse scheme for Tehran. The model minimizes the total cost of wastewater collection, conveyance, treatment and distribution, subject to hydraulic, capacity and demand constraints. It selects branch points on existing trunk sewers (diameter ≥ 1200 mm), routes flow by gravity to local treatment packages sited next to parks, and meets irrigation demand in full. The model was solved with CPLEX and verified on a reduced instance whose optimum was established by complete enumeration. All demands of 38 parks are met through 49 gravity-fed routes from 47 manholes. Charging local treatment at 10,000 tomans per cubic meter, the scheme repays its capital in 3.8 years and cuts the 15-year cost by 65.8% against the centralized alternative; the advantage holds below 58,333 tomans per cubic meter. The findings provide a scalable framework for embedding decentralized reuse within urban water planning for water-scarce megacities.

title: Automation Defect Detection Using High Resolution Ultrasound in Honeycomb Sandwich Panels
summary: Abstract This study presents an automated ultrasonic inspection method for detecting and quantifying interface defects in honeycomb composite laminate sandwich panels. Using immersion-based pulse-echo ultrasonic testing with full RF-wavefor
content: Abstract This study presents an automated ultrasonic inspection method for detecting and quantifying interface defects in honeycomb composite laminate sandwich panels. Using immersion-based pulse-echo ultrasonic testing with full RF-waveform capture, ultrasonic data was acquired from Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) panels with a Nomex honeycomb core. Typical interface defects are created, such as missing adhesive, embedded Kapton and polytetrafluorethylene (PTFE) films, and missing core sections, with defects ranging in size from 4.7 mm to 40.8 mm. Two automation strategies to quantify the planar dimensions of the defect were developed: the first using the energy of the interface reflection and the second utilizing an effective facesheet thickness measurement based on the front and back wall reflections. Defect areas were extracted through image thresholding, and their shape was extracted and quantified via a custom algorithm implemented in MATLAB. Results show that the interface energy based detection method (EBD) achieved a consistently higher accuracy, with defect sizing errors typically below 1 mm with a maximum of 1.9 mm over all specimens investigated. In contrast, the thickness-based detection method (TBM) provided excellent accuracy for Kapton inserts (errors less than 0.65 mm) but exhibited larger deviations, up to 4.2 mm, for holes and PTFE defects due to a poor backwall signal. Results are presented that suggest that the backwall echo can be used for defect identification type. The automated techniques for dimensionalization demonstrated good performance across a wide defect size range, with a reliable detection and quantification of features as small as 4.7 mm and provide a reliable alternative to manual signal analysis.

title: The Digital Clean Development Nexus Across Emerging Economies
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: The monograph argues that emerging economies can leapfrog carbon‑intensive development by tightly integrating digital public infrastructure, IoT telemetry, and edge automation with clean energy systems. As stated in the executive thesis, di
content: The monograph argues that emerging economies can leapfrog carbon‑intensive development by tightly integrating digital public infrastructure, IoT telemetry, and edge automation with clean energy systems. As stated in the executive thesis, digital systems are “the primary catalysts required to overcome persistent structural deficits,” enabling countries to slash grid losses, coordinate distributed solar‑battery fleets, and unlock real‑time climate hazard warnings. This digital‑clean nexus reverses the traditional industrialization sequence: instead of building physical assets first and optimizing later, nations embed computational intelligence upfront to decouple economic growth from resource consumption. Chapters 1–4 demonstrate how digitalization transforms core energy and industrial systems. Smart grids equipped with AMI and feeder telemetry collapse AT&C losses from >30% to single digits, breaking what the text calls a “debilitating financial insolvency spiral” for utilities. Industrial IoT paired with variable‑frequency drives eliminates thermal waste and reduces process energy per tonne by more than half, supported by “continuous sensor feedback loops” that deliver a 61% net reduction. Virtual Power Plants (VPPs) aggregate rooftop solar, commercial batteries, and flexible loads into cloud‑orchestrated dispatchable capacity, displacing fossil peaker plants and extending battery life through AI‑managed thermal balancing. The monograph emphasizes that digital infrastructure is not optional—it is a precondition for clean energy diffusion. As Chapter 1 notes, “clean energy investments face severe friction” when digital adoption remains below critical thresholds, because utilities cannot absorb variable renewables, banks cannot verify generation data, and payment systems cannot support distributed asset financing. Conversely, interoperable digital rails—identity, payments, telemetry, and open APIs—unlock commercial scaling of clean technologies across power, industry, mobility, agriculture, and supply chains. Across its 12‑chapter analytical architecture, the monograph presents a unified strategic mandate: national governments must harmonize digital and energy regulation, enforce open standards, and treat digital telemetry as essential public infrastructure. The result is a 2026–2050 roadmap where emerging economies achieve climate‑resilient growth by replacing capital‑intensive physical expansion with software‑coordinated efficiency, distributed generation, and real‑time intelligence.

title: Enhancing wear resistance of tool steel materials for industrial automobile component using cryogenic treatment
summary: The durability of sheet metal punching tools depends largely on their wear resistance and frictional behaviour during service. Deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) has emerged as an effective post-heat-treatment process for improving the tribolog
content: The durability of sheet metal punching tools depends largely on their wear resistance and frictional behaviour during service. Deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) has emerged as an effective post-heat-treatment process for improving the tribological performance of tool steels. This study experimentally investigates the influence of DCT on the wear characteristics and service life of three commercially used tool steels, namely EN31, AISI D2, and OHNS, employed for punching and piercing 4.5 mm thick SAPH440 sheet steel. The tool steels were conventionally heat treated, deep cryogenically treated at − 196 °C for 18 h and subsequently tempered. Their tribological behaviour was evaluated using a pin-on-disc wear test under dry sliding conditions at a load of 140 N. Wear, wear resistance, wear coefficient, frictional force, and coefficient of friction were determined for each material. The tribological performance of EN31, D2, and OHNS tool steels improved significantly after conventional heat treatment with tempering (CHTWT) and deep cryogenic treatment with tempering (DCTWT) compared with the raw condition. The average wear decreased by 91% for EN31, 86.5% for D2, and 87% for OHNS after conventional heat treatment. Following deep cryogenic treatment, the wear reduction further increased to 94% for EN31, 98% for D2, and 93% for OHNS compared with the untreated specimens. DCT followed by tempering improved the tribological performance of all the investigated tool steels. Among them, AISI D2 exhibited the best overall performance, with the lowest average wear (26 μm), highest wear resistance (4.67), lowest wear coefficient (2.91 × 10 −5 ), lowest average frictional force (14 N), and lowest coefficient of friction (0.10). Compared with the conventionally heat-treated condition, the wear resistance of D2 increased by 517%, while the average wear decreased by 85%. SEM analysis was performed to examine the worn surfaces, while industrial punching trials were conducted to assess tool life under actual operating conditions. SEM observations revealed shallow wear grooves and a homogeneous martensitic matrix with finely dispersed carbide particles, consistent with the improved wear behaviour. Industrial punch life was highest for D2 (3765 min), followed by EN31 (3130 min) and OHNS (2665 min). The results demonstrate that DCT followed by tempering is an effective post-heat-treatment process for enhancing the tribological performance and service life of industrial tool steels, with AISI D2 providing the best overall performance for SAPH440 sheet metal punching applications.

title: GETP v1.0: Global Energy Transition Pace Database - realised ascent and descent rates for electricity technologies in 214 countries, 1985–2025
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: GETP v1.0 is a harmonised database of realised ascent and descent rates for electricity technologies in 214 countries over 1985–2025. WHAT IT DOES DIFFERENTLY Research on the pace of energy transitions has developed almost entirely on the g
content: GETP v1.0 is a harmonised database of realised ascent and descent rates for electricity technologies in 214 countries over 1985–2025. WHAT IT DOES DIFFERENTLY Research on the pace of energy transitions has developed almost entirely on the growth side. How fast solar and wind can expand has been characterised in detail; how fast coal, oil and gas actually contract has not been measured with the same instrument, on the same sample, at the same time. GETP applies a single, model-agnostic diagnostic engine symmetrically to expanding and contracting trajectories, so that the two halves of a transition can be compared on like terms. CONTENTS - 166,388-observation harmonised panel: 214 countries × 14 technologies and aggregates × two measurement bases (share of national generation, and generation per person) × 1985–2025- 5,680 diagnosed country–technology–basis series with 110 variables each- Country-level summary (716 variables) and a 58-variable core subset- World reference series and world-level diagnostics- Full codebook (824 entries), automated validation report, Excel bundle- Complete build and analysis code ASCENT METRICS Takeoff year (three thresholds), first inflection point, benchmark growth rate, maximum growth rate with bootstrap confidence interval, growth pulses, post-inflection cruising speed, best sustained 3/5/10-year rates, threshold-crossing times, and a logistic reference fit. DESCENT METRICS (the novel component) Peak year with 95% bootstrap confidence interval and peak probability, descent onset, descent inflection, benchmark decline rate, maximum decline rate with confidence interval, descent cruising speed, rebound episodes, decline half-life, phase-out year, and projected phase-out at each country's own demonstrated speed. Every descent metric is also computed on a post-2000 window, because a technology's all-time peak often predates the policy-relevant turning point. DERIVED COUNTRY INDICATORS Ascent–descent asymmetry indices, displacement ratios (full record and last decade), and a five-level transition stage classification. VALIDATION Seven automated internal consistency checks pass. Externally, the ascent engine reproduces published estimates from an independent research group: restricted to grids above 10 TWh, GETP gives a median benchmark growth rate of 0.706 pp/yr for wind against a published 0.656 (IQR 0.372–1.460), and 0.797 for solar against a published 0.713 (IQR 0.292–1.922). Both fall inside the published interquartile ranges. Face-validity checks recover documented national histories (UK coal, US coal, German nuclear, Chinese coal, Danish fossil, Vietnamese solar). REPRODUCIBILITY Derived entirely from two openly licensed Our World in Data files. No proprietary input. The whole database regenerates bit-identically from a clean extract with a single command in roughly 20 seconds. SHA-256 hashes of the source files are recorded at build time. title: How Clean Technology Diffusion Can Reshape Global Development
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Clean technology diffusion is fundamentally rewriting the development model of the Global South. Historically, economic growth and carbon emissions moved in lockstep, forcing emerging economies into a costly fossil‑fuel industrialization pa
content: Clean technology diffusion is fundamentally rewriting the development model of the Global South. Historically, economic growth and carbon emissions moved in lockstep, forcing emerging economies into a costly fossil‑fuel industrialization pathway. As the monograph states, “clean technologies have become substantially cheaper to build, faster to deploy, and cheaper to operate than fossil fuel alternatives.” This monograph demonstrates that falling costs in modular clean technologies—solar PV, LFP batteries, electrolyzers, heat pumps—are enabling a structural decoupling of GDP growth from carbon emissions. Wright’s Law learning curves have driven 80–90% cost collapses across key clean capital goods, allowing latecomer economies to leapfrog directly into low‑carbon industrialization without bearing early‑stage R&D costs. Across power systems, decentralized solar‑storage mini‑grids now outperform centralized grid extension beyond ~7 km, delivering electricity at $0.08–$0.11/kWh and enabling productive rural electrification. In mobility, electric two‑ and three‑wheelers paired with battery swapping achieve TCO parity within six months, raising driver incomes by 30–45% and slashing petroleum imports. Agriculture is transformed through solar irrigation, cold‑chain hubs, and bio‑fertilizers, raising smallholder incomes by 40–60% while eliminating diesel dependence. Heavy industry transitions through industrial heat pumps, thermal storage, and ultra‑cheap green hydrogen corridors in Chile, Namibia, India, and Egypt—unlocking green steel, green ammonia, and competitive clean manufacturing. Digital grid modernization—smart inverters, BESS peakers, edge‑AI virtual power plants—expands renewable hosting capacity from 18% to over 80% while halving transmission losses. At the macroeconomic level, clean diffusion becomes a sovereign balance‑of‑payments defense, retaining over $635 billion in foreign exchange reserves by 2035 through petroleum import substitution. The monograph concludes with a 10‑year national clean development roadmap (2026–2035), sequencing decentralized power, fleet electrification, mineral value‑addition, grid digitalization, and sovereign de‑risking finance. Clean technology diffusion emerges not as an environmental agenda but as the supreme macroeconomic growth strategy of the 21st century—enabling emerging economies to achieve sovereign resilience, industrial competitiveness, and permanent economic convergence.

title: Cooling the Global South Without Worsening Global Warming
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: The monograph argues that cooling is now a core development determinant across the Global South, yet its rapid expansion threatens to trigger severe electric grid stress, refrigerant-driven climate forcing, and urban heat island amplificati
content: The monograph argues that cooling is now a core development determinant across the Global South, yet its rapid expansion threatens to trigger severe electric grid stress, refrigerant-driven climate forcing, and urban heat island amplification. As incomes cross the Cooling S‑Curve threshold, air‑conditioner adoption accelerates exponentially—projected to expand from 1.5 billion to 4.5 billion units by 2050, with over 80% of growth in emerging economies. Without intervention, peak cooling demand in EMDEs will rise from 320 GW to 2,950 GW, consuming up to 20% of the remaining 1.5°C carbon budget. To prevent this collision, the monograph synthesizes a 12‑pillar national cooling architecture integrating thermodynamics, refrigerant chemistry, passive building science, grid flexibility, cold chain resilience, and financial innovation. It demonstrates that: Natural refrigerants (R‑290, R‑744) can eliminate >99% of refrigerant warming potential, but require updated safety standards and technician certification. “Operating annual leakage represents an astonishing 52% of total lifetime F‑gas impact…” Super-efficient inverter ACs cut electricity use by 66%, with paybacks under two years, yet remain under‑adopted due to market failures and environmental dumping. Passive cooling envelopes—cool roofs, shading, insulation, ventilation—reduce indoor temperatures by 8–12°C and cut cooling loads 24–45%, often at <$3/m². “Uninsulated tin roofs act as massive radiant heaters… elevating indoor daytime temperatures up to 8°C above outdoor ambient levels.” District cooling systems deliver COPs >6.5 and shift 45% of peak load through thermal storage, transforming cooling into a grid‑stabilizing utility. Agricultural and healthcare cold chains—solar cold rooms, PCM storage, Solar Direct Drive fridges—reduce food loss by 70–80% and ensure vaccine integrity during 96‑hour outages. Demand-side flexibility (ADR, TOU tariffs, smart thermostats) avoids $18.5B in peaker plant capex across major megacities. Bulk procurement and Cooling‑as‑a‑Service collapse price premiums by 38%, democratizing access to efficient cooling. The monograph concludes with a National Cooling Action Plan (NCAP) framework that unifies cross‑ministerial governance and establishes 2030–2050 milestones for MEPS ratcheting, Kigali refrigerant transition, passive building codes, cold chain deployment, and grid flexibility. Full implementation yields 116 Gt CO₂e in cumulative abatement and $500B/year in consumer electricity savings by 2050. Cooling, when redesigned as an integrated national system, becomes not a climate liability but a pillar of thermal resilience, economic productivity, and sustainable development across the Global South.
