title: International climate finance and emission reductions: what do the last twenty years tell us?
summary: Abstract We empirically examine the impact of international climate finance transfers on recipient countries’ carbon emissions. We analyse the effect of mitigation and adaptation finance using emission data of 164 non-OECD countries from 20
content: Abstract We empirically examine the impact of international climate finance transfers on recipient countries’ carbon emissions. We analyse the effect of mitigation and adaptation finance using emission data of 164 non-OECD countries from 2000 to 2017. We use a distributed lag model in first differences, a panel method that allows us to abstract from possible feedback from current emissions to future transfers. We address potential reverse causality while accounting for dynamic effects. We control for other factors that could be correlated with both climate finance flows and emissions. Contrary to expectations, we find that public mitigation finance tends to increase emissions, potentially due to some misreporting of development aid as climate finance. Public adaptation finance appears to drive an even greater increase in emissions. We explain this by the energy-intensive nature of adaptation measures. Transfers under the Clean Development Mechanism reduce emissions modestly after five years.

title: Análisis de los parámetros de ajuste del motor para operación con biodiésel
summary: The utilization of biofuels such as biodiesel in internal combustion engines often results in increased specific fuel consumption and higher emissions of certain pollutants, particularly nitrogen oxides (NOx). This study conducts a systemat
content: The utilization of biofuels such as biodiesel in internal combustion engines often results in increased specific fuel consumption and higher emissions of certain pollutants, particularly nitrogen oxides (NOx). This study conducts a systematic and analytical review to explore and organize various engine adjustment strategies aimed at mitigating these drawbacks. The review focuses on recent literature addressing the influence of compression ratio, exhaust gas recirculation (EGR), and injection timing. The analysis reveals that retarding injection timing and implementing EGR are the most effective techniques for reducing NOx emissions, albeit potentially leading to an increase in carbon monoxide (CO) emissions. In contrast, increasing the compression ratio contributes to improved thermal efficiency. The study concludes that combining two or more techniques such as EGR with injection timing adjustments or operating under lean-burn conditions is essential to simultaneously achieve optimal engine performance and effective NOx emission reduction.

title: Exploring thrifting practices among Generation Z in greater Jakarta: a perspective on social practices and environmental communication
summary: Generation Z in Greater Jakarta engages with thrifting as an everyday communicative practice through which ideas about sustainability are understood and expressed. This study examines this practice through Social Practice Theory, Sustainabl
content: Generation Z in Greater Jakarta engages with thrifting as an everyday communicative practice through which ideas about sustainability are understood and expressed. This study examines this practice through Social Practice Theory, Sustainable Consumption Theory, Media Ecology Theory, and Attribution Theory. Using a qualitative interpretivist design and reflexive thematic analysis, the study draws on in depth interviews with seven purposively selected participants. Their accounts indicate that thrifting is associated with affordability, product quality, identity expression, environmental awareness, and engagement with digital media. Participants also recognized the environmental benefits of secondhand clothing while considering broader consequences of imported thrift products, including transportation emissions, implications for local textile industries, and global waste circulation. Instagram and TikTok emerged as communicative spaces where sustainable fashion became more visible through algorithmic exposure, peer interaction, and user generated content. Across these accounts, sustainability was not understood solely as an environmental concern. It was connected to economic value, cultural identity, environmental responsibility, and experiences with digital media in everyday thrifting practices. The study contributes to environmental communication scholarship by showing how meanings of sustainable fashion are shaped through the intersection of consumption, communication, and digital media in a Global South context.

title: Canadian 2023 and 2025 Boreal Forest Wildfires: Downwind Formaldehyde to Nitrogen Dioxide Ratios and Implications for Surface Ozone Formation
summary: The Canadian boreal forest wildfires of 2023 and 2025 set new records for area burned and resulted in extensive emissions of trace gases such as formaldehyde (HCHO), nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ), and carbon monoxide (CO). Surface ozone formatio
content: The Canadian boreal forest wildfires of 2023 and 2025 set new records for area burned and resulted in extensive emissions of trace gases such as formaldehyde (HCHO), nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ), and carbon monoxide (CO). Surface ozone formation has been shown to be driven by variations in HCHO-to-NO 2 concentration ratios (FNRs), with FNRs showing ozone sensitivity to NO 2 and volatile organic compound (VOC) concentrations. We use TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI) measurements to analyse enhancement rates and vertical column density enhancements (∆VCDs) of FNRs downwind of 26 wildfire plumes from 2023 and 2025 in Western and Central Canadian boreal forests. Fires from 2023 and 2025 showed similar enhancement rates downwind for HCHO, NO 2 , and CO, consistent with previous studies using this method. The majority of FNRs showed sensitivity to VOCs near the source of the smoke and a rapid transition (within an hour of emission) to sensitivity to NO 2 as the plume aged, downwind, consistent with in-situ and model-based studies. As sensitivity of ozone formation to NO 2 occurs downwind, cities in the path of wildfire smoke could have increased ozone-related public health risk due to enhanced NO 2 in cities.

title: Environmental Pollution in Food Production and Pathways for Mitigation through Sustainable and Circular Approaches
summary: Abstract Global food production is under increasing pressure to meet global food security demands while simultaneously reducing environmental burdens. This review critically evaluates air emissions, greenhouse gas (GHG) contributions, water
content: Abstract Global food production is under increasing pressure to meet global food security demands while simultaneously reducing environmental burdens. This review critically evaluates air emissions, greenhouse gas (GHG) contributions, water pollution, and solid waste generation across the entire food production life cycle, including agricultural production, food processing, and associated waste management. Over its entire life cycle, global food production contributes approximately 58% of anthropogenic PM 2.5 emissions, and 72% ammonia ( NH 3 ), underscoring its substantial impact on air quality. In addition, irrigation activities alone contribute nearly 70% of global freshwater withdrawals, while the food manufacturing sector accounts for about 30% of total industrial water consumption, highlighting the sector’s intensive water demand. Food loss and waste (FLW) further exacerbate environmental burdens, with landfill disposal responsible for an estimated 58% of fugitive methane emissions from municipal landfills due to food waste decomposition. This review synthesizes mitigation strategies including resource recovery (nutrient, energy, material), low-energy approaches, zero liquid discharge (ZLD), sustainable agricultural practices, and advancements in food processing technologies. By integrating environmental performance, technology readiness level (TRL), and implementation barriers, this review advances beyond existing studies that focus on isolated processes and identifying key bottlenecks and research gaps; the study provides practical insights to support the development of environmentally responsible and resource-efficient food production.

title: Oxidative Enhancement of Polystyrene Bioconversion Associated with Bio-Fenton-Type Processes in a Mesocosm-Scale Plastivore System
summary: Abstract Sustainable plastic waste management calls for mesocosm-scale biological strategies coupling polymer depolymerization with controlled plastic-carbon transformation, yet routes for optimizing plastivore-mediated bioconversion beyond
content: Abstract Sustainable plastic waste management calls for mesocosm-scale biological strategies coupling polymer depolymerization with controlled plastic-carbon transformation, yet routes for optimizing plastivore-mediated bioconversion beyond laboratory scale remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a mesocosm-scale plastivore-based platform using Tenebrio molitor larvae and show that moderate Fe supplementation increased the •OH-associated oxidative activity, accompanied by enhanced polystyrene (PS) depolymerization and PS disappearance. Under a simplified incineration-reference scenario, the estimated PS-derived carbon conversion flux corresponded to a gross avoided direct-emission potential of up to approximately 0.31 t CO2 per ton of larvae per month, without representing net life-cycle greenhouse gas mitigation. Molecular analyses showed greater oxidative functionalization, oligomer formation, and chain scission than under regular bioconversion. Quantitative •OH assays and fluorescence imaging further showed stronger intestinal •OH-associated levels, faster signal development, and earlier stabilization in the enhanced bioconversion system. Together, the evidence supports Fe-mediated enhancement of intestinal oxidative processes consistent with bio-Fenton-type reactions and identifies redox modulation as a promising and scalable strategy for plastic depolymerization and bioconversion.

title: Effects of Greenhouse Gas Emission on Agricultural Production and the Prospects of Their Sequestration with Biochar
summary: Production of biochar involves pyrolysis of nearly any carbon (cellulose-lignin) feedstock under oxygen-limited conditions. This can include waste from forestry, agriculture, animal farming, and industry. Biochar is a highly calcitrant carb
content: Production of biochar involves pyrolysis of nearly any carbon (cellulose-lignin) feedstock under oxygen-limited conditions. This can include waste from forestry, agriculture, animal farming, and industry. Biochar is a highly calcitrant carbonaceous material. There are numerous agricultural and environmental uses for this potentially cheap, carbon-negative resource. Adding biochar to soil is still one of the most significant uses for it. It enhances the physical and biochemical soil characteristics and raises its fertility and productivity. Ultimately, it may also improve the pH, microbial activity, aggregation, and water retention of the soil, all of which contribute to the overall quality of the soil. The impact of biochar is more apparent in soil with a coarse texture, while there is a lot of variation based on the kind of biochar, soil, crops and environmental conditions. The impact of biochar is more apparent in soil with a coarse texture, while there is a lot of variation based on the kind of biochar and soil, crop, and environment conditions. Applying biochar on a long-term basis can increase soil productivity and nutrient retention, which eventually lowers the requirement for chemical fertilizers. Biochar also contributes to the improvement of soil biological quality by increasing soil aeration, soil moisture, and soil productivity. The amount that biochar affects the physiochemical qualities of soil varies according to several factors, including the cropping system, size, kind, and source of the biochar.

title: Oil pollution and water quality in Awoye, Nigeria: Total petroleum hydrocarbon and microbial assessment
summary: This study assessed the health implications of oil pollution in Awoye, Ondo State, Nigeria, through the evaluation of Total Petroleum Hydrocarbons (TPH) and microbial contamination in surface and borehole water sources. Results showed that
content: This study assessed the health implications of oil pollution in Awoye, Ondo State, Nigeria, through the evaluation of Total Petroleum Hydrocarbons (TPH) and microbial contamination in surface and borehole water sources. Results showed that surface water was more heavily impacted by hydrocarbon pollution than borehole water, with hydrocarbon profiles indicating recent petrogenic contamination. Microbial analyses revealed total coliform and fecal coliform counts exceeding World Health Organization (WHO) safety standards in both water sources, while the detection of E. coli confirmed ongoing fecal contamination. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) identified anthropogenic petroleum activities as the primary source of contamination, with additional contributions from natural and combustion-related sources. Health risk assessment indicated hazard index values below the threshold of concern for non-carcinogenic chemical effects in both adults and children, although children demonstrated relatively greater exposure vulnerability. Despite the low chemical risk, the presence of pathogenic microorganisms and hydrocarbon pollutants represents a significant threat to water quality and community well-being. The findings underscore the need for improved water treatment, enhanced sanitation practices and continuous environmental monitoring to reduce contamination and protect public health in oil-impacted coastal communities.

title: Automated Product Carbon Footprint Estimation via Low-Latency Neural Language Processing in Multilingual, Real-Time Supply Chains
summary: Real-time product carbon footprint (PCF) reporting is increasingly required in global supply chains, yet conventional life cycle assessment (LCA) remains difficult to scale due to fragmented multitier data, heterogeneous formats, and substa
content: Real-time product carbon footprint (PCF) reporting is increasingly required in global supply chains, yet conventional life cycle assessment (LCA) remains difficult to scale due to fragmented multitier data, heterogeneous formats, and substantial manual effort. This article proposes Auto-LCA, a system-level architecture for continuous, product-level carbon estimation that integrates (i) automated supply-chain data acquisition, (ii) low-latency multilingual natural language processing for extracting life-cycle-relevant attributes from unstructured documents, (iii) a structured product carbon data model, and (iv) machine-learning-based completion of missing life cycle inventory parameters with provenance and confidence tags. A central mechanism is the "carbon header," which packages accumulated embodied and operational emissions as transferable, version-controlled metadata associated with product identifiers and propagated incrementally across supply-chain tiers. Auto-LCA is designed as an open Application Programming Interface (API) layer to interface with enterprise systems (e.g., ERP/PLM/MES) and supports update-driven recomputation that recalculates only affected nodes in the supply-chain graph, improving scalability for large product portfolios and deep supplier networks. Case studies in the steel, cement, and automotive sectors demonstrate that Auto-LCA yields estimates close to representative conventional LCA benchmarks (typically within ±4%), while enabling broader coverage and more frequent updates under realistic data availability constraints. The framework also aligns with emerging digital product passport and sustainability reporting needs by enabling traceable, machine-readable carbon metadata exchange across organizations.

title: Effects of Ammonia Substitution and Fuel Injection Strategy on Non-Premixed Methane–Air Swirl Flames
summary: The use of ammonia (NH3) as a carbon-free fuel is a promising pathway for low-carbon combustion, but its low reactivity and high NOx formation present significant challenges for stable operation and emissions control. In swirl-stabilized no
content: The use of ammonia (NH3) as a carbon-free fuel is a promising pathway for low-carbon combustion, but its low reactivity and high NOx formation present significant challenges for stable operation and emissions control. In swirl-stabilized non-premixed systems, the effects of fuel injection strategy, swirl intensity, and NH3/CH4 blending remain insufficiently understood. This study presents a systematic experimental comparison of three fuel injection configurations (radial, axial, and central-rod) on the stability and emission characteristics of NH3/CH4/air swirl flames. Experiments covered NH3 fractions from 0% to 100% at two swirl numbers (Sn = 0.8 and 1.4), with equivalence ratio (0.6–1.2) variations at 50% NH3 and Sn = 1.4. Emissions (NOx, CO, CO2, H2) are measured using gas analyzers, complemented by optical diagnostics for flame structure assessment. Results show that injector configuration is a key parameter governing both flame stability and pollutant formation. Radial injection provides the widest stability range and enables stable combustion up to 100% NH3, attributed to enhanced recirculation and improved flame anchoring. In contrast, axial and central-rod configurations exhibit reduced stability limits and earlier flame destabilization with increasing ammonia content. A trade-off between stability and emissions is observed, with radial injection enhancing flame stability. Increasing NH3 substitution reduces measured NOx emissions at high ammonia fractions, but the associated rise in H2 and changes in CO/CO2 suggest reduced combustion efficiency and possible incomplete NH3 oxidation. These findings highlight fuel injection strategy as a key parameter for balancing stability and emissions in NH3/CH4 combustion systems.

title: HYpersaline Plume Emission and Risk from CO₂ Storage (HYPER-CO2)
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Pressure management is an important part of maintaining the integrity and storage capacity of carbon dioxide storage reservoirs. In saline aquifer storage systems, this may require the production and disposal of reservoir brines. These brin
content: Pressure management is an important part of maintaining the integrity and storage capacity of carbon dioxide storage reservoirs. In saline aquifer storage systems, this may require the production and disposal of reservoir brines. These brines can be hypersaline, hot, anoxic, enriched in metals or organic contaminants, and potentially acidified by elevated CO₂ content. In their undiluted form, they may pose a risk to marine ecosystems, but natural mixing in energetic shelf seas can substantially reduce their impact potential. This study builds on previous work by assessing not only hypersaline brine release, but also a wider hazard-screening source term based on high-end North Sea produced-water and CCS-relevant formation-water properties. A high-resolution FVCOM hydrodynamic model was used to simulate seabed and sea-surface brine release scenarios. The modelled brine fraction was then used to estimate dilution and compare predicted concentrations against regulation-informed screening thresholds for selected hazardous constituents. Results show that the impacted area increases non-linearly with dilution threshold. At lower dilution thresholds, affected area increases rapidly, but at higher thresholds the footprint begins to level off. The most demanding dilution requirements are associated with benzene, zinc, lead, arsenic, and phenol, representing intentionally conservative worst-case screening scenarios and not expected to occur as a chemically coherent release from a single reservoir; rather, it is designed to test the upper bound of potential dilution requirements. Overall, the results indicate that natural shelf-sea mixing can substantially reduce brine-release impacts, but site-specific assessment remains essential.

title: Catalyst or constraint? Academic independent directors and corporate consciousness of climate change under ESG practice
summary: This study investigates the role of academically experienced independent directors (AIDs) in shaping firms’ climate risk consciousness in Chinese listed companies. Using a panel dataset from 2008 to 2023 and fixed effects regression models,
content: This study investigates the role of academically experienced independent directors (AIDs) in shaping firms’ climate risk consciousness in Chinese listed companies. Using a panel dataset from 2008 to 2023 and fixed effects regression models, we find that a higher proportion of AIDs significantly enhances firms’ climate risk consciousness. The effect operates through two mechanisms: improving the quality of corporate information disclosure and shaping executives’ environmental cognition. The influence of AIDs is stronger in firms with low managerial ownership, weaker internal ESG performance, higher analyst coverage, and in regions with stricter environmental regulations. The study contributes to the literature by examining the previously underexplored impact of AIDs on corporate environmental awareness, identifying key moderating factors, and highlighting the role of China’s Confucian cultural context in shaping board effectiveness. These findings provide practical implications for policymakers and corporate practitioners regarding board composition and the integration of academic expertise to promote corporate sustainability.

title: Decarbonization Roadmap: Prioritized Mitigation Hierarchy in the Paint and Coating Industry
summary: Anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from chemical manufacturing present substantial operational, compliance, and competitive challenges under international climate accords and emerging regulatory frameworks, including the European
content: Anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from chemical manufacturing present substantial operational, compliance, and competitive challenges under international climate accords and emerging regulatory frameworks, including the European Union Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM). This study provides an empirically grounded, multi-site decarbonization framework combining longitudinal quarterly operational datasets collected from 14 industrial coating manufacturing facilities (2024–2025) with an audited baseline manufacturing facility producing 35,640 metric tonnes annually. Lifecycle GHG accounting reveals that upstream raw material procurement and synthesis (Category 4) dominate the value-chain carbon footprint, contributing 89.48% (172,557 tCO2e) of the total 192,834 tCO2e baseline organizational footprint. In contrast, direct stationary combustion (Category 1) and purchased electricity (Category 2 location-based) account for only 0.89% (1711 tCO2e) and 2.46% (4741 tCO2e), respectively. To resolve implementation trade-offs, a Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) framework integrates annual carbon abatement potential, Technology Readiness Level (TRL), capital intensity, and payback dynamics to establish a prioritized Six-Tier Decarbonization Hierarchy: Tier 1 (Priority 1)—upstream bio-based resin and binder substitution, delivering an estimated baseline reduction of 25,880–60,050 tCO2e/year (13.4–31.1% of baseline emissions); Tier 2 (Priority 2)—drop-in bio-based and circular solvent replacement, achieving 4820–9640 tCO2e/year (2.5–5.0% baseline reduction); Tier 3 (Priority 3)—thermal process electrification via high-temperature industrial heat pumps (COP 2.5–3.1), eliminating 1027–1369 tCO2e/year; Tier 4 (Priority 4)—contractual and on-site renewable electricity procurement via corporate Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) and solar PV (4490–4741 tCO2e/year; 2.3–2.5% baseline reduction); Tier 5 (Priority 5)—systemic formulation transitions to waterborne, high-solids, and powder coating architectures (15,000–35,000 tCO2e/year); and Tier 6 (Priority 6)—stream-conditional Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS), strictly restricted to concentrated combustion stacks (CO2 ≥ 8 vol%) and excluded from dilute post-thermal oxidizer off-gases (CO2 ≤ 1–4 vol%) where capture is economically unviable ($180–$260/tCO2e).

title: Energy conversion technologies for climate mitigation: A quantitative cross‐technology and sector analysis
summary: Abstract Energy conversion technologies are fundamental to decarbonizing global energy systems, yet their widespread adoption is hindered by high costs, infrastructure gaps, and poor cross‐sector integration. This paper provides a novel cro
content: Abstract Energy conversion technologies are fundamental to decarbonizing global energy systems, yet their widespread adoption is hindered by high costs, infrastructure gaps, and poor cross‐sector integration. This paper provides a novel cross‐technology comparative framework through an integrated quantitative assessment of hydrogen production, solar thermal systems, bioenergy, and CO 2 conversion technologies, evaluating their technical readiness, scalability, and system integration potential using unified techno‐economic metrics and a cross‐sectoral framework. The analysis reveals that hydrogen offers 66–95% global warming reduction potential and $10.0–15.7 trillion USD in climate mitigation cost savings, alongside a 600 Mt. annual CCUS capacity gap by 2030. While several conversion technologies have reached technical maturity (TRL 7–9), realizing chemical‐sector CCU potential would require over 18,100 PWh (55% of projected global supply) of low‐carbon electricity. A cross sector integration framework links electrification (40%‐), CCUS (30%, 1.49 Gt CO 2 /yr), and circular economy strategies (16%) for hard‐to‐abate industries. The findings provide actionable quantitative insights for corporate sustainability planning, R&D portfolio optimization, and infrastructure investment decisions, emphasizing that widespread deployment depends on continued cost reductions, successful pilot to commercial scaling, and strategic modernization of energy infrastructure to achieve net zero emissions by mid‐century. The overarching objective is to guide strategic decision‐making for net‐zero transitions by providing a unified evidence base for prioritizing investments across competing technology pathways.

title: Electrospun membranes based on cellulose nanomaterials for advanced water treatment applications
summary: Access to safe drinking water remains a major challenge, especially in regions lacking centralized treatment. Cellulose nanomaterials (CNMs) offer renewable, biodegradable options for membranes with improved hydrophilicity, strength, and fo
content: Access to safe drinking water remains a major challenge, especially in regions lacking centralized treatment. Cellulose nanomaterials (CNMs) offer renewable, biodegradable options for membranes with improved hydrophilicity, strength, and fouling resistance. This review summarizes cellulose extraction, CNM production, and membrane fabrication methods, emphasizing electrospinning as a versatile strategy for multifunctional water treatment. CNM-based electrospun membranes show strong promise, though broader adoption requires sustainable solvents, scalable production, and cost-effective manufacturing innovations.

title: Solar‐tracking PV ‐assisted hybrid drying for low‐carbon apple dehydration: Energy–exergy performance and CO 2 mitigation
summary: Abstract This study experimentally evaluated a solar‐tracking PV‐assisted hybrid dryer for low‐carbon apple dehydration through an integrated assessment of drying kinetics, energy and exergy performance, auxiliary grid‐electricity demand, a
content: Abstract This study experimentally evaluated a solar‐tracking PV‐assisted hybrid dryer for low‐carbon apple dehydration through an integrated assessment of drying kinetics, energy and exergy performance, auxiliary grid‐electricity demand, and operational CO 2 mitigation. The system combined a single‐axis tracking flat‐plate solar air collector, a separate PV‐powered ventilation and control subsystem, a 5‐kW auxiliary electrical heater, and a forced‐convection drying chamber. Red Delicious apple slices of 3 and 6 mm thickness were dried at 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 m s −1 under a nominal drying‐air temperature of 50°C. Increasing air velocity accelerated moisture removal, reducing drying time from 240 to 135 min for 3‐mm slices and from 300 to 180 min for 6‐mm slices, but increased the auxiliary electrical requirement. The lowest airflow provided the greatest grid‐energy displacement relative to the analytically estimated fully electrical baseline, with electrical energy reduction ratios of 86.39% and 87.15% for 3‐ and 6‐mm slices, respectively. The maximum avoided operational emission reached 1.334 kg CO 2 batch −1 for 6‐mm slices at 0.5 m s −1 , whereas the highest specific carbon saving was 2.899 kg CO 2 kg −1 dried product for 3‐mm slices under the same airflow condition. Exergy analysis further characterized the thermodynamic performance of the tracking collector and the physical exergy behavior of the drying‐air stream across the chamber. Overall, the investigated configuration demonstrated a clear operating trade‐off between rapid dehydration and reduced auxiliary grid‐electricity demand, with low airflow favoring carbon mitigation and higher airflow favoring shorter processing time.

title: A centralised green computing course for digital researchers
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Abstract: Digital research covers a wide range of disciplines, and researchers have very different levels of technical experience. When we started designing a course on digital research sustainability, one of our main challenges was making
content: Abstract: Digital research covers a wide range of disciplines, and researchers have very different levels of technical experience. When we started designing a course on digital research sustainability, one of our main challenges was making sure it would be relevant to people from different backgrounds. To address this, we developed four personas (case studies) that represent common digital research roles: a Research Software Engineer, a computational lab researcher, an HPC user, and a machine learning practitioner. The first part of the course introduces key concepts and terminologies for green computing, while the second part uses these case studies to encourage participants to reflect on how the ideas apply to their own work. The iterations of the course that we have run so far, have attracted diverse audiences, from computational researchers to sustainability professionals. Their feedback has helped to further improve the course materials. As a positive outcome of developing this course, Imperial’s sustainability team have also launched a university-wide seven steps to ICT sustainability. In this talk, I will share some of the experiences the team had while developing and delivering this course. The audience will have the opportunity to reflect on and provide feedback on the topic. Some questions to consider would include: What are the pros and cons of adapting such a course to different research groups or disciplines under a wider institutional setting? What other approaches could RSEng teams take when (developing and) delivering digital research sustainability training? When considering the impact of digital research, should we stick to accounting for the carbon emissions only or also focus on other types of environmental impacts as well (e.g. water)?

title: 集成系统电子管理：工程生物
summary: AbstractWe integrated three major functional modules—Engineering Biological Carbon Fixation and Energy Storage (EBCFES), Biomass Gasification Power Generation and Chemical Polygeneration Project (BGPCP), and Mechanism for Effectively Reduci
content: AbstractWe integrated three major functional modules—Engineering Biological Carbon Fixation and Energy Storage (EBCFES), Biomass Gasification Power Generation and Chemical Polygeneration Project (BGPCP), and Mechanism for Effectively Reducing Atmospheric CO₂ Concentration (MCERCC)—into an integrated system (Integrated System EBM, or EBM). Through systematic design and leveraging the leverage effect of energy gain enhancement, improve the energy storage and carbon fixation efficiency of biological systems, and use this as a unified optimized solution to compare with and complement traditional electrical energy storage methods. Integrate carbon fixation, energy production, energy storage, and comprehensive utilization of biomass—especially emission reduction and carbon reduction mechanisms—into a strategic framework for achieving carbon rebalancing.
